resources.name: AFLOW
resources.summary: Duke-led repository of DFT-calculated properties for millions of inorganic compounds and prototypes (4+ million entries reported in 2021), including thermodynamic, electronic and mechanical properties.
resources.access: Web search; AFLUX REST API for programmatic queries (no key); AFLOW prototype encyclopedia and online tools.
resources.notes: Query syntax (AFLUX) has a learning curve; like all high-throughput DFT databases, values are computed, not measured.

resources.name: CAS Common Chemistry
resources.summary: Free, authoritative subset of the CAS REGISTRY covering nearly 500,000 substances: CAS numbers, names, structures and basic properties, released under CC BY-NC 4.0.
resources.access: Web interface; free API after registering at cas.org/services/commonchemistry-api.
resources.notes: Non-commercial license (CC BY-NC 4.0); only a small fraction of the full ~200-million-substance CAS Registry, which remains a paid product (SciFinder).

resources.name: CCDC Access Structures
resources.summary: Free CCDC/FIZ Karlsruhe service to search, view and download individual deposited crystal structures (CIF files) from the Cambridge Structural Database and ICSD by DOI, deposition number, name or basic search.
resources.access: Web interface; retrieve CIFs one structure at a time; depositing your own structures is also free.
resources.notes: The full CSD (bulk database, ConQuest, Mercury advanced features, CSD Python API) requires a paid institutional license; the free route is deliberately limited in how many structures you can view and retrieve, and has no substructure/statistical search.

resources.name: ChEMBL
resources.summary: EMBL-EBI's manually curated database of drug-like bioactive molecules: ChEMBL 36 (Sept 2025) covers ~2.8 million distinct compounds, 17,803 targets and over 24 million bioactivity measurements extracted from the literature.
resources.access: Web interface; full database dumps (SQLite/PostgreSQL/MySQL) for download; Python via `pip install chembl_webresource_client`.
resources.notes: Data released under CC BY-SA 3.0; releases come roughly yearly, so pin the release number in any published analysis.

resources.name: ChemSpider
resources.summary: Royal Society of Chemistry structure database linking over 130 million structures to properties, spectra, vendors and literature from hundreds of data sources.
resources.access: Web interface (structure, name and property search); developer API via RSC developer portal.
resources.notes: Web search is free without an account; the API requires a key from the RSC developer portal and has call quotas. It is an aggregator, so verify critical values against the underlying source.

resources.name: Crystallography Open Database (COD)
resources.summary: Fully open collection of ~535,000 crystal structures of organic, inorganic, metal-organic compounds and minerals (Aug 2026), all downloadable as CIF with no restrictions.
resources.access: Web search; full database mirrorable via rsync/HTTP; MySQL dumps; also queryable through the OPTIMADE API.
resources.notes: Coverage overlaps with but is far smaller than the licensed CSD/ICSD; quality varies since entries come from many sources, though curation scripts are applied.

resources.name: JARVIS (NIST)
resources.summary: NIST's Joint Automated Repository for Various Integrated Simulations: JARVIS-DFT holds ~40,000 3D and ~1,000 2D materials with around a million calculated properties (band gaps incl. meta-GGA, elastic, dielectric, topological), plus force-field and ML datasets.
resources.access: Web apps (free sign-up); datasets downloadable via `pip install jarvis-tools` (e.g. `jarvis.db.figshare.data('dft_3d')`).
resources.notes: Smaller than Materials Project/AFLOW but includes properties (spin-orbit spillage, TBmodels, 2D exfoliation energies) the others lack.

resources.name: MassBank (Europe)
resources.summary: First public repository of reference mass spectra for small molecules: ~120,000 spectra of ~18,500 compounds from 53 contributors (2026), with a redesigned web interface launched in 2025.
resources.access: Web search (spectrum, peak, substructure); complete data versioned on GitHub (MassBank/MassBank-data) with DOI-assigned releases.
resources.notes: Complementary siblings exist (MassBank of North America has a larger but differently curated collection); check license per record (mostly CC BY).

resources.name: Materials Cloud
resources.summary: EPFL/MARVEL open-science platform: a moderated archive for computational materials datasets with DOIs, curated databases (e.g. MC3D/MC2D crystal structures), interactive tools, and full AiiDA provenance graphs for reproducing workflows.
resources.access: Web interface; archive records downloadable without an account; free registration to submit datasets.
resources.notes: Archive submissions are moderated for scope (computational materials science); browsing provenance graphs requires understanding AiiDA concepts.

resources.name: Materials Project
resources.summary: DFT-computed properties (formation energies, band structures, elasticity, phase diagrams) for over 150,000 inorganic materials, run by LBNL; database updated regularly (v2026.04.13 current as of mid-2026).
resources.access: Free account gives an API key; Python client `pip install mp-api` (e.g. `MPRester(API_KEY).materials.summary.search(...)`); interactive web apps; bulk data also on AWS Open Data.
resources.notes: Computed (PBE/r2SCAN) values, not experimental — band gaps are systematically underestimated; API has rate limits but they are generous for individual use.

resources.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook
resources.summary: NIST Standard Reference Database 69: evaluated thermochemical properties, ion energetics, IR/UV-Vis/mass spectra, and thermophysical fluid properties for thousands of organic and small inorganic species.
resources.access: Web interface (search by name, formula, CAS number, structure); no bulk download.
resources.notes: No API or bulk export; NIST formally reserves the right to charge for access in the future, though it has been free for decades.

resources.name: nmrshiftdb2
resources.summary: Community NMR database with ~45,000 structures and ~54,000 measured spectra (plus ~450,000 including calculated), offering free 13C/1H chemical-shift prediction and peak/structure search under an open-content license.
resources.access: Web interface for search and prediction; open data downloads; contributions accepted after free registration.
resources.notes: Prediction quality depends on how well your scaffold is represented in the community-contributed data.

resources.name: NOMAD
resources.subcategory: FAIR repository for computational materials data
resources.summary: Open repository and archive for raw input/output files of atomistic calculations: more than 13 million entries from 60+ simulation codes (VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO, FHI-aims, GW, DMFT, MD), uploaded by hundreds of groups.
resources.access: Web browse/download without an account; free registration to upload (each upload gets a DOI); REST API and Python package `pip install nomad-lab`.
resources.notes: Aimed at reproducibility and data publishing rather than quick property lookup; parsing quality varies by code.

resources.name: Open Reaction Database (ORD)
resources.summary: Open schema and repository for structured organic reaction data (conditions, yields, procedures), including large USPTO-derived reaction sets and high-throughput experimentation datasets, built for machine-learning use.
resources.access: Web search at client.open-reaction-database.org; raw data (protobuf) in the ord-data GitHub repo; schema tools via `pip install ord-schema`.
resources.notes: Data licensed CC-BY; coverage is dominated by patent-mined and donated HTE datasets, so it is not a comprehensive reaction encyclopedia like the commercial Reaxys/SciFinder.

resources.name: OPTIMADE
resources.summary: A common REST API specification implemented by most major materials databases (Materials Project, AFLOW, OQMD, COD, NOMAD, JARVIS, Materials Cloud and others), letting one query format search many databases.
resources.access: HTTP GET against each provider's /v1/structures endpoint with a shared filter grammar (e.g. filter=elements HAS ALL "Ti","O"); Python tools via `pip install optimade`.
resources.notes: You still need to understand each provider's coverage and property vocabulary; the spec covers structures well, properties less uniformly.

resources.name: OQMD (Open Quantum Materials Database)
resources.summary: Northwestern (Wolverton group) database of DFT-calculated thermodynamic and structural properties for ~1.4 million materials, strong on formation energies and ground-state phase stability.
resources.access: Web interface; RESTful and OPTIMADE APIs; full database downloadable as a MySQL dump; Python via the `qmpy` package.
resources.notes: Full-database download is tens of GB; web interface is spartan compared with Materials Project.

resources.name: PubChem
resources.summary: NIH's open chemistry database: roughly 119 million compounds and 322 million substances aggregated from over 1,000 sources (2025 update), with bioactivities, properties, spectra links, patents and literature annotations.
resources.access: Web interface; PUG-REST API (no key needed, e.g. https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/rest/pug/compound/name/aspirin/property/CanonicalSMILES/JSON); bulk download via FTP; Python via `pip install pubchempy`.
resources.notes: API politeness limits (no more than ~5 requests/second); bulk users should use the FTP dumps rather than hammering the REST API.

resources.name: SDBS (Spectral Database for Organic Compounds)
resources.summary: AIST (Japan) database of measured spectra for ~34,000 organic compounds: 1H/13C NMR, IR, Raman, EI-MS and ESR; a standard free lookup for compound identification.
resources.access: Web interface (search by name, formula, mass, or peak positions).
resources.notes: Daily access limits apply per user; some collections (e.g. Raman) are no longer updated; no bulk download.

resources.name: ZINC-22
resources.summary: UCSF Irwin/Shoichet lab database of tens of billions of commercially available (make-on-demand) molecules in docking-ready 2D/3D formats, searchable by similarity, substructure and supplier code.
resources.access: CartBlanche web interface; bulk subsets via direct download, Globus, and AWS/OCI cloud mirrors.
resources.notes: Run on academic best-effort infrastructure — large downloads can be slow; 3D conformers are precomputed with specific protonation assumptions you should check for your use case.

resources.name: AiiDA
resources.summary: Open-source (MIT) Python infrastructure for automating high-throughput atomistic calculations while recording the full provenance graph of every input, code and output; plugins exist for Quantum ESPRESSO, VASP, CP2K and many others.
resources.access: `pip install aiida-core` plus a plugin (e.g. `aiida-quantumespresso`); results shareable on Materials Cloud.
resources.notes: Real setup cost (PostgreSQL, message broker, daemon); pays off for hundreds+ of calculations, overkill for a handful.

resources.name: ASE (Atomic Simulation Environment)
resources.summary: Python library (LGPL) for setting up, steering and analyzing atomistic calculations with a uniform `Atoms` object and calculator interfaces to dozens of codes (VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO, GPAW, LAMMPS, xtb, ML potentials).
resources.access: `pip install ase`; e.g. `from ase.build import bulk; atoms = bulk('Cu')` then attach any calculator.
resources.notes: ASE itself computes nothing expensive — you still need a backend DFT/forcefield code or an ML potential for real energies.

resources.name: Avogadro
resources.summary: Open-source (BSD) cross-platform molecular builder/editor used to sketch molecules in 3D, set up input files for quantum chemistry codes (ORCA, Gaussian, GAMESS) and visualize outputs and orbitals.
resources.access: Direct download of installers for Windows/macOS/Linux from avogadro.cc; no account needed.
resources.notes: Avogadro 2 is the actively developed line; some legacy plugins from Avogadro 1.x are still being ported.

resources.name: CP2K
resources.summary: Open-source (GPL) quantum chemistry and solid-state package built around the mixed Gaussian and plane-waves method; the workhorse for ab initio molecular dynamics of condensed-phase systems (liquids, interfaces).
resources.access: Source and binaries via cp2k.org; `conda install -c conda-forge cp2k`; input decks are text files run with `cp2k.x`.
resources.notes: Input format is verbose and idiosyncratic; the online input reference and tutorials are essential.

resources.name: LAMMPS
resources.summary: Sandia's open-source (GPL-2) classical MD code, the standard for materials simulation: metals, polymers, granular systems, coarse-grained models, and now ML interatomic potentials; scales from one laptop core to the largest supercomputers.
resources.access: `conda install -c conda-forge lammps`, distro packages, or build from source; driven by text input scripts (`lmp -in in.script`).
resources.notes: You must supply/choose interatomic potentials yourself (see OpenKIM); script language takes time to learn — the matsci.org LAMMPS forum is the support channel.

resources.name: NWChem
resources.summary: PNNL's open-source (ECL 2.0) computational chemistry package covering molecular HF/DFT/coupled cluster and plane-wave DFT in one code, designed to scale to large parallel machines.
resources.access: `conda install -c conda-forge nwchem` or distro packages; text input files run via `nwchem input.nw`.
resources.notes: Documentation is thinner than ORCA/Psi4; its niche is combined molecular+periodic capability and MPI scaling.

resources.name: Open Babel
resources.summary: Open-source (GPL-2) toolbox that interconverts on the order of 100 chemical file formats and provides fingerprints, forcefield 3D coordinate generation and batch processing — the field's universal adapter.
resources.access: `conda install -c conda-forge openbabel` or distro packages; CLI: `obabel input.smi -O output.sdf --gen3d`; Python bindings via the `openbabel` module.
resources.notes: Development pace has slowed; for pure Python workflows RDKit covers much of the same ground with a more active community.

resources.name: OpenMM
resources.summary: Open-source, GPU-first molecular dynamics engine with a clean Python API and support for custom forces; extremely fast on a single consumer GPU, widely used for biomolecular and increasingly for ML-potential simulation.
resources.access: `conda install -c conda-forge openmm`; Python: build a System from PDB + force field and run with a Simulation object.
resources.notes: Sits on the chemistry/biophysics boundary — for inorganic/hard-matter MD, LAMMPS is usually the better fit; a CUDA/OpenCL GPU makes a huge speed difference.

resources.name: ORCA
resources.subcategory: quantum chemistry package (free binaries for academia)
resources.summary: Widely used quantum chemistry program (DFT, DLPNO-CCSD(T), multireference, spectroscopy) from the Neese group/MPI KoFo, free of charge for academic research and teaching, with over 90,000 registered academic users; current release ORCA 6.x.
resources.access: Register a free account on the ORCA forum (orcaforum.kofo.mpg.de), then download binaries for Linux/macOS/Windows.
resources.notes: Closed source; the no-cost license is worded around academic use at academic institutions — commercial use requires a paid FACCTs license, and unaffiliated researchers should read the current EULA before relying on it.

resources.name: Psi4
resources.summary: Open-source (LGPL-3) quantum chemistry package: HF, DFT, MP2, coupled cluster (CCSD(T)), SAPT and more, usable as a program or as a Python module; runs fine on a laptop for small and medium molecules.
resources.access: `conda install -c conda-forge psi4`; Python: `import psi4; psi4.energy('b3lyp/cc-pvdz')` on a molecule block.
resources.notes: Memory/CPU hungry beyond ~50 heavy atoms with correlated methods, as with any ab initio code; excellent education resources via PsiCode and Psi4Education.

resources.name: pymatgen
resources.summary: The Materials Project's open-source (MIT) Python library for materials analysis: structure/symmetry manipulation, phase diagrams, Pourbaix diagrams, electronic structure analysis, and I/O for VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO, CIF and many other formats.
resources.access: `pip install pymatgen`; pairs with `mp-api` to pull Materials Project data straight into Structure objects.
resources.notes: Tight coupling to Materials Project conventions (e.g. energy corrections) — read the docs before mixing with your own DFT numbers.

resources.name: PySCF
resources.summary: Apache-2.0 quantum chemistry framework written mostly in Python: molecular and periodic HF/DFT, MP2, CCSD, CASSCF, with an architecture designed for method development and hacking.
resources.access: `pip install pyscf`; `from pyscf import gto, scf; scf.RHF(gto.M(atom='H 0 0 0; H 0 0 0.74', basis='sto-3g')).kernel()`.
resources.notes: Aimed at people comfortable with electronic-structure theory; less hand-holding than Psi4 or ORCA.

resources.name: Quantum ESPRESSO
resources.summary: Open-source (GPL) suite for plane-wave pseudopotential DFT: ground states, band structures, phonons (DFPT), molecular dynamics; the most common free code for periodic solids.
resources.access: Source from quantum-espresso.org or GitLab; `conda install -c conda-forge qe`; run via `pw.x < input.in`; ASE and pymatgen can generate inputs.
resources.notes: Steep learning curve (pseudopotentials, k-points, cutoffs); small systems run on a laptop but production work usually needs a cluster.

resources.name: RDKit
resources.summary: The de facto standard open-source cheminformatics library (BSD-3): SMILES/mol parsing, substructure search, fingerprints, descriptors, 2D depiction, 3D conformer generation, reaction handling; C++ core with Python bindings.
resources.access: `pip install rdkit` (official wheels) or conda-forge; `from rdkit import Chem; Chem.MolFromSmiles('CCO')`.
resources.notes: API is large and some behavior (sanitization, aromaticity models) surprises newcomers; the RDKit blog/Cookbook are essential reading.

resources.name: VESTA
resources.summary: Standard tool for visualizing crystal structures, electron/charge densities and crystal morphologies; reads CIF and most DFT code outputs, produces publication-quality figures.
resources.access: Direct download for Windows/macOS/Linux from jp-minerals.org.
resources.notes: Free of charge but not open source; distributed free for academic, scientific, educational and non-commercial users (commercial users currently also tolerated at no cost).

resources.name: xtb (GFN-xTB)
resources.summary: Grimme group's open-source (LGPL) semiempirical quantum chemistry code implementing GFN1/GFN2-xTB and GFN-FF: geometry optimizations, conformer energies and frequencies for systems of hundreds of atoms in minutes on a laptop.
resources.access: `conda install -c conda-forge xtb`; CLI: `xtb molecule.xyz --opt`; pairs with CREST for conformer sampling.
resources.notes: Semiempirical accuracy — great for screening, geometries and conformers, not a replacement for DFT/coupled-cluster energies.

resources.name: ChemRxiv
resources.summary: The chemistry community's preprint server, co-owned by ACS, RSC, GDCh, CCS and the Chemical Society of Japan; free to submit and read, with DOIs assigned and screening within days.
resources.access: Web interface; free account to submit; reading requires nothing.
resources.notes: Migrated from Cambridge Open Engage to Wiley's Research Exchange Preprints platform in January 2026 — same chemrxiv.org address. Check individual journal policies, though essentially all major chemistry journals now accept preprinted work.

resources.name: Organic Syntheses
resources.summary: Since 1921, detailed organic synthesis procedures that have each been independently repeated and checked in a Board of Editors member's lab; 2,500+ articles covering well over 5,000 reactions, all free online.
resources.access: Web interface with keyword and structure search; free PDF download of every procedure back to 1921.
resources.notes: Coverage is selective (reliable, broadly useful procedures) rather than comprehensive.

resources.name: ACCESS (US NSF cyberinfrastructure allocations)
resources.summary: NSF program allocating free time on US supercomputers (Expanse, Bridges-2, Delta, Anvil and others); entry-level 'Explore' allocations need only a short abstract, and graduate students may be PIs with an advisor's letter.
resources.access: Create an ACCESS account, submit an Explore request (a few paragraphs) at allocations.access-ci.org; awards are exchanged for credits on specific machines.
resources.notes: US-based researchers affiliated with a US academic institution, nonprofit or FFRDC only — genuinely unaffiliated researchers are not eligible; larger tiers require progressively more justification.

resources.name: ChemCompute
resources.summary: Free web gateway (NSF-supported) that runs GAMESS quantum chemistry, TINKER and NAMD molecular dynamics jobs on real HPC resources (Expanse, Bridges-2) with both guided student modes and a raw input-file researcher mode.
resources.access: Register free at chemcompute.org (academic email recommended), submit jobs via web forms or uploaded input files.
resources.notes: Built for undergraduate teaching and research; fair-use queueing rather than guaranteed allocations — heavy production users should seek proper allocations (e.g. ACCESS).

resources.name: nanoHUB
resources.summary: NSF-funded Purdue platform where hundreds of nanotechnology and materials simulation tools (including DFT and semiconductor device tools) run in the cloud through your browser, alongside 1,000+ courses and learning modules.
resources.access: Free account, then launch tools directly in the browser — no local install.
resources.notes: Per-session compute is modest — good for education, prototyping and small research jobs, not production HPC campaigns.

resources.name: ARKIVOC
resources.summary: Free journal of organic chemistry published by the non-profit ARKAT USA since 2000: no charges for authors or readers, CC-BY licensed, thousands of peer-reviewed articles.
resources.access: Submit via arkat-usa.org; all content free to read.
resources.notes: Lower impact-factor prestige than society flagships; solid, legitimate venue for organic chemistry without funding.

resources.name: Beilstein Journal of Organic Chemistry
resources.summary: Peer-reviewed diamond/platinum open-access journal fully financed by the non-profit Beilstein-Institut: no APCs for authors, no paywall for readers, publishing continuously since 2005.
resources.access: Submit via the journal website; read freely.
resources.notes: Sister title Beilstein Journal of Nanotechnology runs the same no-fee model. Notable context: RSC's Chemical Science, diamond OA since 2015, introduced an APC from 1 July 2026 — making the Beilstein journals and ARKIVOC among the few remaining truly free-to-publish venues in chemistry.

resources.name: LiveCoMS (Living Journal of Computational Molecular Science)
resources.subcategory: diamond OA living reviews & best practices
resources.summary: Diamond open-access journal (no fees for authors or readers, CC BY) publishing 'living' best-practice guides, tutorials and software comparisons for molecular modeling, maintained as versioned documents on GitHub.
resources.access: Read free on livecomsjournal.org; submissions are LaTeX documents developed in public GitHub repos.
resources.notes: Its best-practices articles (MD setup, free-energy calculations, force-field selection) double as some of the field's finest free learning material.

resources.name: ACS Petroleum Research Fund (UR/UNI grants)
resources.summary: ACS-administered endowment funding fundamental research related to petroleum/energy; its Undergraduate Research (UR) and Undergraduate New Investigator (UNI) tracks specifically fund faculty at non-doctoral, often modestly resourced institutions.
resources.access: Proposals submitted by the institution through the ACS PRF portal in annual cycles.
resources.notes: Grants go to nonprofit institutions, not individuals — unaffiliated researchers are not eligible; research must have a plausible connection to the petroleum field, and the PI must hold a faculty-equivalent appointment.

resources.name: Experiment.com
resources.summary: All-or-nothing crowdfunding platform dedicated to scientific research with a dedicated chemistry category; projects are reviewed for scientific merit before launch and the platform reports roughly a 48% funding success rate.
resources.access: Create a project page on experiment.com; no institutional affiliation required.
resources.notes: 8% platform fee plus ~3-5% payment processing on funded projects; realistic raises are typically in the $1k-15k range — good for consumables and small equipment, not salaries.

resources.name: RSC Researcher Development and Travel Grants
resources.summary: Royal Society of Chemistry grants of up to £500 per person for activities that develop you as a researcher (conferences, courses, collaboration visits), open to RSC members worldwide including early-career grades (AMRSC).
resources.access: Online application in scheduled rounds via rsc.org; requires current RSC membership.
resources.notes: Membership dues apply (heavily discounted for students); from 2026 Round 2, Affiliate-grade members lose eligibility — Associate Member (AMRSC) or higher is the safe grade. RSC also runs larger Research Enablement and Researcher Collaborations grant schemes.

resources.name: Deep Learning for Molecules and Materials (dmol.pub)
resources.summary: Andrew White's free online book on machine learning for chemistry and materials: graph neural networks, equivariances, generative models, with every chapter as runnable Jupyter code.
resources.access: Read in the browser; run chapters via the included Colab/Jupyter links; source on GitHub.
resources.notes: Assumes working Python and some ML background; the fast-moving field means some chapters lag the latest architectures.

resources.name: LibreTexts Chemistry
resources.summary: The largest open chemistry textbook collection: full remixable texts across general, organic, inorganic, physical, analytical and biological chemistry, plus lab manuals and interactive exercises, used as the primary text at many institutions.
resources.access: Web, no account needed; pages exportable to PDF.
resources.notes: Quality varies page to page since content is community-remixed; the flagship texts (e.g. the general and organic chemistry cores) are solid.

resources.name: MIT OpenCourseWare (Chemistry & Materials Science)
resources.summary: Free materials from 2,500+ MIT courses, including complete lecture videos and problem sets for core chemistry (5.111/5.112, 5.61 quantum, thermodynamics) and materials science (3.091 Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry).
resources.access: Web, no registration; videos also on YouTube; materials downloadable.
resources.notes: No credit, graded feedback or certificates; some older courses lack video.

resources.name: MolSSI Education
resources.summary: Free workshop-style lessons from the NSF Molecular Sciences Software Institute: Python scripting for computational chemistry, software best practices, workflows and QM programming projects, all openly licensed.
resources.access: Work through the lessons in a browser; materials on GitHub.
resources.notes: Note MolSSI's separate Software Fellowship program (US grad students/postdocs) is suspended for 2026-2027; the education materials remain fully available.

resources.name: Chemistry Stack Exchange
resources.summary: The general-purpose chemistry Q&A site of the Stack Exchange network, covering conceptual, organic, inorganic, physical and analytical chemistry questions with a large searchable archive.
resources.access: Read without an account; free account to participate.
resources.notes: Homework-style questions are moderated strictly; research-level computational questions get better answers on Matter Modeling SE.

resources.name: matsci.org (Materials Science Community Discourse)
resources.summary: Discourse forum co-managed by the Materials Project and OpenKIM that hosts the official user forums for LAMMPS, pymatgen, Materials Project, OVITO, OpenKIM and other materials codes — developers answer directly.
resources.access: Read without an account; free registration to post.
resources.notes: This replaced several old mailing lists (e.g. lammps-users); the long-running Computational Chemistry List (CCL) shut down in late 2025, with its archive preserved on Zenodo.

resources.name: Matter Modeling Stack Exchange
resources.summary: Stack Exchange site dedicated to matter modeling: DFT settings, basis sets, quantum chemistry codes (Quantum ESPRESSO, VASP, ORCA, Psi4), force fields and method choice, answered by practising computational scientists including code developers.
resources.access: Read without an account; free account to ask/answer.
resources.notes: Smaller than the big SE sites, so niche questions can take days; searching existing answers is often enough.
